title: Terraform Safety, Team Workflow, and CI/CD
subtitle: Team guardrails for Terraform change safety from PR to controlled apply

nodes.label: Version Control
nodes.definition: Version control stores Terraform code history and makes changes reviewable.
nodes.whyItMatters: Infrastructure changes become auditable, repeatable, and easier to roll back or investigate.
nodes.safeSentence: Putting Terraform in version control makes infrastructure changes reviewable and auditable.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not treat Terraform files as private local scripts that bypass team review.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Version control is the starting point for safe Terraform teamwork because infrastructure changes need history, review, and traceability.

note.summary: Terraform should be handled like application code: branches, PRs, review, and traceability to change intent.

image.caption: From code change to approved apply with state, locking, policy, and blast-radius guardrails.

nodes.label: Pull Request
nodes.definition: A pull request is a review gate for Terraform code changes.
nodes.whyItMatters: It lets teammates review configuration before infrastructure is changed.
nodes.safeSentence: Pull requests give teams a chance to review Terraform changes before they are applied.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not approve a Terraform pull request without understanding the plan impact.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Pull requests help teams review Terraform changes as code before they become real infrastructure changes.

note.summary: Good PR questions: what changed, why, which environment, what does plan show, and any destroy impact?

nodes.label: Format and Validate
nodes.definition: Format and validate are automated checks for Terraform style and basic configuration correctness.
nodes.whyItMatters: They catch simple problems before a plan or review.
nodes.safeSentence: fmt and validate are early quality checks before plan review.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not confuse validate with safety approval. Validate does not prove the change is safe.
nodes.interviewAnswer: A CI pipeline can run terraform fmt and terraform validate to catch formatting and configuration issues before plan review.

note.summary: Typical checks: terraform fmt -check and terraform validate. They reduce noise before plan review.

nodes.label: Plan Review
nodes.definition: Plan review means inspecting Terraform's proposed changes before apply.
nodes.whyItMatters: The plan shows what Terraform intends to create, change, or destroy.
nodes.safeSentence: The Terraform plan is the key evidence for what the change will actually do.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not treat the plan as noise or skip it in production workflows.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Plan review is the main Terraform safety checkpoint because it shows the actual proposed infrastructure changes before execution.

note.summary: Check create/update/delete actions, replacements, environment/backend context, and unexpected scope.

nodes.label: Apply Control
nodes.definition: Apply control limits who or what can run Terraform apply, especially in shared or production environments.
nodes.whyItMatters: Apply changes real infrastructure, so it needs approval and protection.
nodes.safeSentence: Production applies should be controlled because Terraform can create, modify, or destroy critical infrastructure.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not let every developer casually apply to production from a laptop.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Teams often control apply through CI/CD, approvals, protected branches, and restricted credentials.

note.summary: Controls often include CI-only apply, protected branches, approval gates, and scoped credentials.

nodes.label: Remote State
nodes.definition: Remote state stores Terraform state in a shared backend instead of one local machine.
nodes.whyItMatters: Team workflows need one trusted state location.
nodes.safeSentence: Remote state lets the team share a single trusted view of Terraform-managed infrastructure.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not let different team members manage the same infrastructure with separate local state files.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Remote state helps collaboration because everyone works against the same Terraform state instead of isolated local copies.

note.summary: Remote state answers: what is managed now, who can access state, and whether state safety controls exist.

nodes.label: Locking
nodes.definition: Locking prevents multiple Terraform runs from writing state at the same time.
nodes.whyItMatters: Concurrent applies can corrupt or confuse state.
nodes.safeSentence: Locking prevents two Terraform runs from modifying state at the same time.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not bypass locks casually just to make a command run.
nodes.interviewAnswer: State locking protects teams by preventing concurrent Terraform operations from colliding.

note.summary: If lock issues happen, confirm no active run before force-unlock style actions.

nodes.label: Least Privilege
nodes.definition: Least privilege means Terraform credentials get only the permissions required.
nodes.whyItMatters: Terraform automation can change real infrastructure, so credentials must be limited.
nodes.safeSentence: Terraform automation should follow least privilege because it can change real cloud resources.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not run all Terraform automation with broad admin credentials by default.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Least privilege reduces risk by limiting what Terraform credentials can change, especially in production.

note.summary: Use separate lower/prod permissions and avoid permanent broad credentials.

nodes.label: CI/CD Pipeline
nodes.definition: A CI/CD pipeline standardizes Terraform checks, plans, approvals, and applies.
nodes.whyItMatters: Automation reduces manual mistakes and makes workflows repeatable.
nodes.safeSentence: CI/CD helps standardize Terraform checks and reduce manual mistakes.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not automate apply without understanding approval, credentials, and environment boundaries.
nodes.interviewAnswer: A Terraform CI/CD pipeline may run fmt, validate, plan, publish the plan for review, and apply only after approval.

note.summary: Typical flow: PR -> checks -> plan artifact -> review -> approved apply.

nodes.label: Policy Checks
nodes.definition: Policy checks enforce rules before Terraform changes are applied.
nodes.whyItMatters: They can block unsafe or non-compliant infrastructure changes.
nodes.safeSentence: Policy checks can prevent unsafe infrastructure changes before they are applied.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not rely only on human memory for every policy rule.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Some teams use policy-as-code or pipeline checks to enforce security, tagging, cost, or compliance rules before apply.

note.summary: Common checks: tags, encryption, public access, region restrictions, approval requirements.

nodes.label: Blast Radius
nodes.definition: Blast radius is the amount of infrastructure or business impact a change could affect.
nodes.whyItMatters: Terraform can create broad changes quickly, so teams need to understand impact before apply.
nodes.safeSentence: Reviewing the Terraform plan helps teams understand the blast radius before applying changes.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not judge risk only by number of lines changed. Small code changes can have large infrastructure impact.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Blast radius review means asking how much the proposed Terraform change could affect before approving it.

note.summary: Ask: how many resources change, any destroy, production impact, rollback clarity, approval needs.

nodes.label: Environments and Workspaces
nodes.definition: Open the previous map that explains environment separation and workspace caution.
nodes.whyItMatters: Team safety depends on knowing which environment, workspace, backend, and approval path is active.
nodes.safeSentence: Terraform safety depends on environment boundaries as much as command knowledge.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not treat this as a safety concept. It is a map doorway.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Environment separation supports team safety by reducing the risk of applying a change to the wrong place.
